summary:
We developed Fading Wilds, a browser game in which players try to save 15 species that vanished or collapsed as their climate changed, starting with the Bramble Cay melomys, the first mammal extinction attributed to human-induced climate change. Set in 2015, the player chooses a refuge for each species, traces real climate trends and decides where it should go, then discovers what really happened.

Every number comes from NASA data: 45 years (1981–2025) of NASA POWER records for 24 places, verified value by value against the NASA API. Trends are tested with statistical methods, and a machine-learning model forecasts each species' key climate variables to 2030 with honest uncertainty ranges (tested on 2021–2025: ±0.35 °C error in mean temperature). A live NOAA El Niño alert shows which species are most at risk today.

This matters because climate change often feels abstract. By turning real Earth observation data into decisions, the game lets students see that climate change is measurable from space, that extinction depends on climate and habitat, and that good forecasts are honest about their uncertainty.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Fading Wilds is a browser game in which players try to save 15 species that vanished or collapsed as their climate changed, starting with the Bramble Cay melomys, the first mammal extinction attributed to human-induced climate change. The game is set in 2015. For each species, the player chooses among three candidate refuges, traces the trends of its key climate signals with real NASA data, answers what the data show, and decides where the species should go. The feedback then reveals what really happened. An in-game computer brings the story to the present: the player opens an “ML” folder, explores each species’ climate forecast up to 2030, receives a real NOAA El Niño alert and recommends a refuge that should remain suitable until 2030.

Behind the game:

  • Data: 45 years (1981–2025) of NASA POWER monthly data (MERRA-2 reanalysis and CERES) for 24 locations. Every value was checked against the NASA API: 119,925 values, all identical.
  • Survival cards: each species is tracked through its 3 most relevant climate indicators, such as temperature, rainfall, humidity, soil moisture or sea temperature. Its ecological requirements were checked against the scientific literature.
  • Statistics: trends are measured with Sen’s slope and the Mann–Kendall test, corrected for autocorrelation (Hamed–Rao), with p-values adjusted for multiple testing (Holm).
  • Machine learning: forecasts to 2030 average six statistical models with a global LightGBM model and provide 50/80/90% prediction intervals. Trained on 1981–2020 and tested on unseen 2021–2025 data, the model’s mean temperature error was ±0.35 °C, and its 80% interval contained the real value 77% of the time.
  • El Niño: NOAA’s Oceanic Niño Index identifies the six species most sensitive to El Niño and powers a live alert (currently +2.46 °C, comparable to 1997 and 2015).
  • All processing runs offline. The game only reads pre-computed files, so it runs instantly in any browser.

What benefits does it have?

  • Real, verifiable science: every number can be traced back to NASA or NOAA and recomputed from archived raw files.
  • Uncertainty in plain language: players see ranges and how reliable they were (“this range was right 8 times out of 10”), not a single number.
  • Critical thinking: climate alone is not enough, because habitat, predators and disease also decide survival.
  • Free and accessible: a static website with no installation, server or account.
  • Reusable: the documented data package, verification scripts and forecasting model can support other educational or conservation projects.

What is the intended impact?
We want students and the public to learn, through play, that climate change can be measured from space, that extinction depends on climate and habitat together, and that a forecast is only useful when it is honest about its uncertainty. Our next steps are to add NASA’s CMIP6 climate projections (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6), integrate the in-game computer into the main game and test it with students in Temuco, Chile.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript (game), Python 3.12 (data, statistics and machine learning), JavaScript/HTML/CSS (in-game computer prototype), SQL (SQLite) and LaTeX (report).
  • Frameworks and libraries: Phaser 4, React 19, Vite, NumPy, LightGBM, scikit-learn and Matplotlib.
  • Data: NASA POWER API, NOAA CPC/PSL climate indices and NASA GISTEMP.
  • Tools: Git/GitHub, Visual Studio Code, Node.js and Playwright. AI coding assistants (Claude, Codex) helped with code and documentation, and all results were verified with automated tests.
  • Hardware: a standard Windows laptop, with no GPU required.

How is your project creative?

  • The data are the gameplay: instead of reading charts about climate change, players make decisions with the same NASA data scientists use.
  • A Pokédex of lost species turns 15 real extinction stories into a collection players care about.
  • The in-game computer with an “ML” folder lets players discover machine learning as a tool inside the story, not as a lecture.
  • A real El Niño alert links the game to what is happening in the ocean right now.
  • Wrong answers teach too: in one case, the climate data point to a coral atoll as the “best” refuge for a cloud-forest toad, and the game explains why habitat matters more than numbers.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific honesty: every value is verified against its source, uncertainty is always shown, and the forecasts are labeled as the project’s own, not as NASA predictions.
  • No future knowledge: because the game is set in 2015, the decisions use only data available up to 2014. The ML was tested without access to the years it predicts.
  • Data limitations: NASA POWER describes ~50 km grid cells rather than microhabitats, so mountain species are compared by change rather than absolute values.
  • Correcting the record: our literature review corrected two errors in the original species brief, and we flag the requirements that lack published evidence.
  • Accessibility: the game runs in any browser with no installation, explains concepts in plain language, and always pairs colors with text labels.
  • Model choice: we tested complex models and chose the combination that performed best on unseen years, rather than the most complex one.

Source code: https://github.com/markzuckerberg44/awin-is-awin/tree/main
